title: Justice

seo.title: Destiny matrix 8 — Justice: meaning of the arcanum
seo.description: 8 in the destiny matrix is the arcanum of Justice: the energy of balance and law. What 8 means, its strong and weak side, how it differs from neighbours.

meaning: The eighth arcanum in the destiny matrix is the energy of balance and law. It weighs without stopping: where what was put in and what came back have met, and where someone has been left short — and it demands that an act and its consequence meet. If 8 stands in your calculation, you are driven by a sense of measure: the inner need for the account to add up and for a word given to be kept.

Being this arcanum means carrying scales inside that never switch off. A tilt and a lie are felt almost physically, and pretending that everything is fine does not work even for the sake of comfort. This gives rare clarity and directness, but it also keeps you tense: where someone else shrugs and forgets, the eighth notices the mismatch and cannot walk past it.

The main drive here is to bring balance back: to straighten what has tilted, to name the price, to close the debt. And the same drive hides the number’s main conflict — the thin line between putting right and punishing. Let the measure shift half a step, and the pull towards truth becomes a thirst for payback, and a clear mind becomes a prosecutor for whom everyone is guilty already.

A strong 8 keeps measure for the sake of clarity and connection: it can settle a matter on its merits, then close the subject and let it go. A weak one turns the same scales into a weapon — it passes sentence on everyone, keeps an endless register of grievances and confuses justice with revenge. The difference is not in how sharp the sense of truth is, but in whether it serves people or stands over them as a judge.

Among its neighbours in the deck, Justice stands sharply apart. The seventh arcanum, The Chariot, takes things by pressure and speed — it rushes ahead and wins through movement; the eighth first stops and asks whether the victory is deserved and who will pay for it. The ninth, The Hermit, goes into silence in order to understand; for the eighth understanding is not enough — it has to decide and hand down a verdict now, and the pause is exactly what it finds hardest to learn.

article.title: The 8th arcanum in the destiny matrix: Justice, the law of your own actions
article.short: 8 in the destiny matrix is the arcanum Justice, the energy of cause and effect. It governs everything where the cause is you: a word spoken, a promise given, a contract signed, a decision taken and whatever came of it. A strong eight makes a person the one trusted to settle a dispute: they keep their word, sense the right measure and can say “I was wrong” without drama. A weak one turns life into a court session with no recess — with loved ones, with the world and with oneself. An eight turns up in the calculation for 83.7% of people, so the main question is usually a different one: where exactly it stands.

seo.title: Destiny matrix 8: the Justice arcanum — meaning, plus and minus
seo.description: Destiny matrix 8 is Justice, the law of your own actions: plus and minus, program 8, tails, money, the couple and five rules from law for an 8.

sections.h2: What 8 means in the destiny matrix

head: Theme
The eight
rows: an act and its consequence, an agreement, responsibility for your own choice
your word as good as a signature, a sense of measure, honesty without cruelty, decisions carried through
keeping score in relationships, grudges with no statute of limitations, harshness, over-responsibility or its flip side
judge actions, not people; answer for what is yours and don’t take on what belongs to others
what have I agreed to — and is that agreement still fair now?

paragraphs: Justice is perhaps the easiest of the major arcana to understand. Even Arthur Edward Waite, creator of the best-known tarot deck, barely interpreted it: the card, he wrote, “carries above all its obvious meanings”. The obvious thing here is the link between an act and its consequence. With the eight, a person discovers that what is said has weight, what is promised has a deadline, and what is done has a price.

Benebell Wen, a lawyer by profession and author of Holistic Tarot, makes it more precise: this is human-made justice. Laws, contracts, rules, fair shares, the courts — everything people invented in order to live together. The larger order of circumstances that a person cannot influence belongs to another card, the Wheel of Fortune, the tenth arcanum. For the eight, Wen borrows a formula from physics, Newton’s third law: “to every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction”. Push the world, and the world pushes back with exactly the same force.

Waite has one more thought that may matter most of all for the eight. The moral principle “which deals unto every man according to his works”, he writes, differs in its essence from the idea of election. A poet’s gift or the capacity to dedicate one’s life to the highest things is not handed out as a reward for merit: “we have them or have not, and their presence is as much a mystery as their absence”. The law of Justice is not involved in either. Hence three conclusions that tell a mature eight from an exhausted one:

ul: **Your zone is actions.** For what you have said, promised, signed and done, the eight asks you to answer in full, with no “it just happened”.
**Misfortune is not a sentence.** A loss, a divorce, someone else’s meanness do not prove that a person “deserved” it. Justice examines deeds; it does not hand out misfortunes by ledger.
**A gift is not a debt.** Love, talent and luck do not have to be worked off, and you do not have to prove you deserve them. That is a different department.

paragraphs: If you come from tarot and read with the Rider–Waite deck, card VIII there is Strength, and Justice comes eleventh. The destiny matrix counts by the older Marseille order: 8 is Justice, 11 is Strength. The card is the same; only the number changes.

It was Waite himself who swapped them, in the deck Pamela Colman Smith drew for him in 1909. He did not explain why — it was done “for reasons which satisfy myself” — and added that the change carries nothing that will signify to the reader. The swap is usually traced to the astrology of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, to which Waite belonged: there Strength was linked to Leo and Justice to Libra, and Leo comes earlier in the zodiac.

The upshot is simple: when you read about “the eighth card” in a book that follows Waite, go by the card’s name, not its number. If you are after Strength, it is on the page for [arcanum 11](/encyclopedia/arcanum/11).

sections.h2: The eight in the plus: the one people trust to settle a dispute
paragraphs: A strong eight shows in the small things. After a trip together, this is the person who splits the costs — and nobody feels hard done by, because the spreadsheet is honest, with no “roughly half each”. They say “tomorrow at ten” and are there at ten, and if they can’t make it, they warn you the day before and suggest another time. In a work conflict people come to them for a fair hearing, and they are capable of telling a friend: “You’re not the one who’s right here.”

In Waite’s fortune-telling list this card stands for equity, rightness, probity — and one more word, “executive”, the power that carries things out. It is more precise than the rest: Justice does not only reach decisions, it enforces them. A mature eight does not get stuck working out who is right. Decided, done: the debt repaid, the apology made, the contract that stopped being fair torn up.

Two more signs of the plus. The first is admitting a mistake matter-of-factly: “I got it wrong; here’s how I’ll fix it”, with no excuses and no self-flagellation. The second is the ability to separate the act from the person: to condemn what was done without writing off the one who did it. That is exactly what sets justice apart from revenge.

The eight feels an imbalance keenly and often takes the side of the weaker party. In the plus it does so in proportion: it files a proper complaint instead of declaring war, and it seeks to put things right, not to humiliate the culprit.

sections.h2: The eight in the minus: a court that has broken down
paragraphs: In the minus, the eight’s sense of justice does not disappear — it breaks. In Waite’s fortune-telling list the reversed card stands for “law in all its departments, legal complications, bigotry, bias, excessive severity”. A number calculated in the matrix has no reversed position, but as a portrait of a broken court the list is accurate: the letter instead of the spirit, a biased judge, a sentence out of proportion to the offence. In life the breakdown looks like this:

ul: **The invisible tally.** The relationship keeps accounts: who gave way how many times, who called first, who took the bins out. While the tally stays silent, all is quiet. Then it is presented in full, years’ worth at once.
**A case with no statute of limitations.** A grievance over unfairness never closes. A story from ten years ago is retried again and again, though everyone else involved moved on long ago.

**Double standards.** The rules are strict for others and flexible for oneself: someone else’s lateness is disrespect, one’s own is circumstances. There is a mirror version too: leniency for others, the maximum sentence for oneself.
**Justice at any cost.** The fight for truth goes on to complete exhaustion, and the aim quietly shifts: no longer to put things right, but to punish.
**All or nothing.** No shades of grey: either perfect or not at all. Hence perfectionism, black-and-white thinking and an inability to accept “good enough”.

**Over-responsibility and its flip side.** Matrix practitioners describe two extremes in the eight, and in practice they are one and the same breakdown: the person takes everything on, stops coping and one day gives up keeping promises altogether.

paragraphs: A trap of its own is the word “deserved”. In the minus, the eight explains everything as justice: “if he fell ill, there must have been a reason”, “if her husband left, it’s her own fault”. That is a mistake both humanly and by the meaning of the arcanum itself: Justice examines actions; it does not hand out misfortunes. Someone else’s misfortune does not prove their guilt, and your own does not prove yours.

And one last thing. A disillusioned eight concludes that “there is no justice in the world”, and that conclusion is more dangerous than any grievance. From there the next step is an easy one: if nobody plays fair, why should I?

sections.h2: Program 8: the scenarios that go round in circles
paragraphs: “Program 8” is one of the most common searches about the eight. There is no separate entity behind it: in the destiny matrix a program is a scenario that repeats with different people and in different circumstances, and “program 8” is an eight that has landed in a karmic point of the chart. In our reading, the programs section reads the karmic task D as the root of the repetition and the centre E as the state that keeps it going. The eight can stand in both points, and one person in five has a program with it — 20.5% of people. How programs work in general is covered [on a separate page](/programs). Below are four loops typical of the eight in particular.

It starts with a request, especially from someone who is “counting on you”. The first move is to say yes before checking your calendar and your strength: to an eight, even a casual “I’ll see” sounds like a signature on a contract. Then the promises outnumber the hours. Some are kept at the expense of sleep, some fall through. Falling through feels like disgrace, and to make up for it, new promises are made.

**Where to break it:** between the request and the answer. “I’ll get back to you tomorrow” is an honest answer for an eight. And set the terms straight away: what exactly, by when, and what happens if it doesn’t work out.

It starts with a sense of unequal contribution — in a couple, a family, a team. The first move is to say nothing and make a note in an invisible column. The finale is an explosion in which a bill for years is presented, and the other person genuinely cannot see where such a sum came from. Now the argument is about the past, and agreeing on the future no longer works.
**Where to break it:** talk about the imbalance while it is small, and agree on a rule — “whoever gets home first cooks” — instead of gathering evidence.

It starts with an injustice — against you or against someone weaker. The first move is an immediate battle on every front: letters, rows, sleepless nights. The finale: your strength runs out, the system has not budged, and the conclusion that “there is no truth” starts to justify your own dishonest moves.

**Where to break it:** in choosing the battle and the means. Not every injustice is your business. And the one that is gets settled with a proportionate tool: a formal complaint, a lawyer, a document.

It starts with a mistake of your own. The first move is the maximum sentence: “I’ve ruined everything, I can’t be trusted.” The finale: the fear of getting it wrong grows so large that decisions are put off, unfinished things pile up and supply fresh grounds for the prosecution.
**Where to break it:** in proportion. A one-pound mistake calls for a one-pound fix, not a year of self-flagellation.

If the eight stands in the karmic task, these loops are the root, and the repetition shows up in different areas of life until the first move changes. If it is in the centre, it is more of a comfort zone: the habit of keeping track of everything and controlling it holds you in the familiar loop because it feels safe there. How your own section reads is shown on [the “Programs” position page](/encyclopedia/position/loops).

sections.h2: Five rules from law that bring the eight into the plus
paragraphs: The eight is the arcanum of law, and lawyers invented the best tools for it long ago. Legal principles were honed over centuries against the very breakdowns Waite listed: bias, bigotry and excessive severity. Turned inwards, they work as safety rules for a person with a heightened sense of justice.

ol: **Hear the other side.** The Roman formula is audiatur et altera pars. Before you reach a verdict, restate the other person’s position so that they agree: “Yes, that’s exactly what I think.” Until you can do that, you are arguing with your own version of them. The presumption of innocence belongs here too: “he was late” does not yet mean “he doesn’t care”.

**No one is a judge in their own cause.** Nemo iudex in causa sua. When you are a party to a dispute, your sense of justice is biased — everyone is built that way. A test: would you pass the same sentence if your friend had done this to a stranger? If not, you need a third party.
**Let the penalty fit the offence.** Ten minutes late is not worth a week of silence. Before you react, put a size on the offence for yourself — “this is a two out of ten” — and respond to a two.

**The statute of limitations.** Even the state does not hear claims forever: under the Russian Civil Code, the general limitation period is three years. Go through your old grievances and decide on each one: either bring your claim now — as a conversation — or close the case.

**A contract, not an oath.** Pacta sunt servanda — agreements must be kept. That is exactly why an eight should make fewer promises, but more precise ones: what, by when, on what terms, and how to get out if circumstances change. A promise with a caveat is honesty shown in advance.

sections.h2: How to tell if you have an 8
paragraphs: Only the calculation gives the full picture: 83.7% of people have an eight in at least one position of the reading, and for the most frequent arcanum the figure is 85%. But three points can be read off the date of birth without a calculator:

ul: **You were born on the 8th or the 26th** (2 + 6 = 8). The eight stands in the calling card, point A, and leads the age scale from birth to 10.
**You were born in August.** The eight is in point B, the spiritual task, and in the decade from 20 to 30.

**You were born in 1979, 1988, 1997, 2006, 2015 or 2024.** The digits of the year add up to 26 or 8 and reduce to an eight: it stands in point C, the material task, and leads the decade from 40 to 50.

paragraphs: The karmic task D and the centre E can also be checked by hand. D is the sum of A, B and C; the centre is the sum of A, B, C and D; if a number is greater than 22, add its digits together. The other positions — money, relationships, the tail — are easier to see in the full calculation. Most often the eight lands in the [chakra map](/encyclopedia/chakra) (for 54.2% of people), on the age scale (44.9%) and in the money section (28.2%). It stands in the centre of the chart for one person in nine, 11.1%: one of the three most frequent numbers in the centre, alongside 6 and 10.

If you have several eights, Justice does not become “double” or “triple”: each eight stands in its own position and answers for its own area. The extreme case is people born on 8 or 26 August 1979, 1988, 1997, 2006, 2015 and 2024 — twelve dates in all. They have an eight in three outer points at once and in three decades: up to 10, from 20 to 30 and from 40 to 50. Yet for all twelve the karmic task is 6, The Lovers, and the centre is 3, The Empress. Justice shapes how they come across and their spiritual and material tasks, while the karmic lesson and the comfort zone belong to other arcana.

sections.h2: The eight in the positions of the matrix
paragraphs: The arcanum has one meaning, but in each point it answers a question of its own. In brackets is the share of people who have an eight in that position or section.

paragraphs.h3: Calling card: born on the 8th or the 26th (6.6%)

paragraphs: The calling card is what people read off you at the door. An eight here comes across as proper and dependable: this is the one chosen as treasurer of the parents’ group chat, as class rep, as referee in a dispute between friends; they are handed the keys and the casting vote. The flip side is the image of a strict, slightly cold person from whom flawlessness is expected and who is not forgiven a single mistake. The task of the calling card is to let yourself be more than a judge: warm, funny, sometimes wrong.

Point B is what a person learns all their life; the talent line also starts here. The eight sets a task of inner honesty in this point: to live by your own law without demanding that the world do the same. Until the lesson is learned, every injustice wounds personally and pulls you into a fight. Once it is learned, your honesty stops depending on whether others are honest, and that is precisely the kind of person who starts setting the rules of the game around them. The decade of this point runs from 20 to 30, the time of your first serious agreements with the world.

Point C is the material side of life. The eight asks you to build it on a transparent footing: declared income, contracts on paper, debts closed on time, honest taxes. In the minus, the same point turns into undocumented deals, property disputes, fines and missed payments. For this eight, order in the paperwork is the foundation. Its decade runs from 40 to 50.

Point D is the main lesson and the root of the programs. An eight here sets the task of learning justice as responsibility rather than as a trial: answering for your own actions, not shifting the blame onto others and not taking on theirs. This position has a curious side effect of the calculation: if your karmic task is 8, your karmic tail is almost certainly [15-5-8](/encyclopedia/karmic-tail/15-5-8), and the centre holds 7, The Chariot. Out of 4,327 such dates since 1900 there are only 55 exceptions — they have the tail [6-14-8](/encyclopedia/karmic-tail/6-14-8) and 16, The Tower, in the centre. On the age scale D leads the decade from 60 to 70.
On these topics the eight has separate, detailed pages; here is just the essence:

ul: **Centre** (11.1%) — a comfort zone where you feel at ease when everything goes by the rules and above board. In detail: [8 in the centre of the matrix](/encyclopedia/position/center/8).

**Money** (28.2%) — income that rests on transparency: a contract, an invoice, an official job. This also covers an eight at the “dollar” point of the money channel, as other charts call the middle of the money line. In detail: [the money channel with an eight](/encyclopedia/position/money/8).

**Relationships** (16.9%) — a union of equals where agreements are spoken out loud. In detail: [8 in relationships](/encyclopedia/position/relations/8) and [8 under the heart](/encyclopedia/position/love_middle/8).

**Talents and profession** (17.0%) — a gift for making sense of rules and judging impartially: law, audit, finance, quality control, mediation, fact-checking, refereeing in sport. In detail: [8 in talents](/encyclopedia/position/profession/8).

paragraphs.h3: Family: lines F, G, H and I

paragraphs: On the family lines the eight speaks of the family law: the family had its rules, its honour, its word, its “this is how we do things”. In the plus this is a gift — a firm inner core and clear values. In the minus it means rules nobody ever discussed, and family scores to settle: who owes whom, who was short-changed. A useful question: which of my family’s rules do I follow without ever having checked them? With children, the eight asks for one thing — that the rules be the same for everyone, parents included. The eight appears in the family gifts section for 19.9% of people, and in the section on parents and children for 18.5%.

Most often the eight stands in the social purpose — for 10.2% of people. This is a role among others: the person around whom it is clear what rules the game is played by — an arbiter, a negotiator, the author of fair regulations, someone both sides trust to divide up a shared venture. In the personal purpose (5.3%) the eight is about words and deeds matching. In the planetary purpose (5.8%) it is the same law on the scale of society: taking part in making the rules fair not only for one’s own.

In the sections on body resource (20.7%) and the way you rest (18.7%), the eight recharges through clarity: matters closed, promises kept, a clear routine. Rest does not come while something is hanging over you — an unpaid bill, an unanswered email, an unfinished report. This is about what restores your energy; it is not medical advice.

For almost half of all people, 44.9%, the eight leads one of the decades. In those years agreements and results come to the fore: what to put on paper, what to revisit, which past decisions it is time to answer for. Which decade it is depends on the point: A — from birth to 10, F — from 10 to 20, B — from 20 to 30, G — from 30 to 40, C — from 40 to 50, H — from 50 to 60, D — from 60 to 70, I — from 70 to 80.

sections.h2: The eight in the karmic tail
paragraphs: An eight stands in the karmic tail for 16% of people. The tail is read in the order M–N–D: entry, mechanism, root. The eight is never the first number — at the entry of the tail the calculation gives only multiples of three. So it has two roles.
**In the middle, as the mechanism**, the eight shows how the scenario turns: through trials, tallies and working out who is right.

ul: [15-8-11](/encyclopedia/karmic-tail/15-8-11) — The Devil, Justice, Strength (4.2% of people). Pressure that the inner court dresses up as lawful: “I’m within my rights.”
[6-8-20](/encyclopedia/karmic-tail/6-8-20) — The Lovers, Justice, Judgement (2.5%). A choice of the heart that is tried for years like a court case.

paragraphs: **At the end, as the root**, the eight is the task of the tail itself.

ul: [15-5-8](/encyclopedia/karmic-tail/15-5-8) — The Devil, The Hierophant, Justice (9.2%, one of the three most common tails). A union, a vow or a family rule that quietly turns into a chain.
[6-14-8](/encyclopedia/karmic-tail/6-14-8) — The Lovers, Temperance, Justice, the rarest of the 26 tails: 55 birth dates since 1900. A home where love little by little turns into management.

paragraphs: In all four tails the eight turns a question of life into a court case. Their way out is shared too: replace the verdict with an agreement. How to read a tail in general is explained in [the karmic tail section](/encyclopedia/position/past_lives).

A personal year with an eight is a time when imbalances rise to the surface and ask to be recounted: who put in how much, what was promised to whom, which agreement has stopped being fair. Decisions made in such a year last a long time. How to calculate your year and what to do with it is on the page [the 8th arcanum for the year](/year/8).

sections.h2: The eight in the couple’s matrix
paragraphs: The compatibility matrix is a third chart put together from two personal ones: the partners’ matching points are added up and reduced to 1–22. In Yuliana Lisovskaya’s school, the eight in it is a union with a cool head and a warm heart: duties are shared fairly, big purchases are decided together, there is a plan B and a reserve, and quarrels pass without scenes. In the minus — living like neighbours, broken promises and responsibility that swells into control. Most often the eight stands in the couple’s home life and in the middle of its tail; what it means at each point is on a separate page about the eight in compatibility. The method gives no compatibility percentages.

If the eight stands in the personal matrix of one of the partners, read it by position — in the [relationships reading](/encyclopedia/position/relations/8) and the [point under the heart](/encyclopedia/position/love_middle/8).

sections.h2: The eight in men and in women
paragraphs: Gender plays no part in the matrix formulas: a man and a woman born on the same day have the same numbers, and the eight means the same for both. Readings “for men” and “for women” usually describe the same traits, only in familiar roles. Whatever the gender, the eight has one trap: if it is used to answering for everyone in the family, care turns into control and high standards into the loneliness of a judge.

What it shares with 8
The difference
rows: Temperance reconciles opposites within a person; Justice, the relations between actions, people and rules
The Wheel is the larger order of circumstances a person cannot influence; the eight, the consequences of your own decisions
the eight reaches a decision by the rules; Judgement is an awakening in answer to a call
both are virtues, and Waite swapped their numbers

The Emperor sets order by his own authority; Justice stands above any authority, his included

paragraphs: How the eight sounds next to a particular arcanum in the same matrix is covered on the combination pages — for example, [8 and 11](/encyclopedia/combination/8-11) or [8 and 14](/encyclopedia/combination/8-14).

sections.h2: Justice in the Waite deck: what the classic card shows
paragraphs: On the card by Waite and Pamela Colman Smith, Justice sits on a throne between two grey pillars. Behind her hangs a dark veil, and above it a yellow sky shows through. She wears a crown, a red robe and a green cloak. In her right hand she holds a sword raised point upwards, in her left a pair of scales, and a white shoe peeps out from under her hem. The number on the card is XI.

Waite hardly analyses the symbolism: the sword and the scales are the traditional signs of justice, and he refers the reader to the historical part of the book. The only thing he dwells on is the pillars. Justice sits between them just as [The High Priestess](/encyclopedia/arcanum/2) does, and Waite takes care to warn that the likeness is deceptive: “the pillars of Justice open into one world and the pillars of the High Priestess into another”. Behind the first lies the moral law by which every man is dealt with according to his works. Behind the second lie mystery and gifts that are not earned but received. This is the very line between deeds and gifts where the eight begins.

Wen adds her own reading of the veil: the curtain is hung up “as if covering or shielding the yellow light of the natural world”, and what remains in front of it is justice made by people. That is why the card is so often linked to laws and courts in the literal sense.

Look at her eyes: they are open, and Justice is looking straight at the viewer. The blindfold familiar from statues of Themis outside courthouses is absent in tarot — and not by chance. In antiquity the goddess of justice was shown with her eyes open. The earliest known blindfolded Justice is a 1494 woodcut for Sebastian Brant’s Ship of Fools, in the chapter on people who go to law over every trifle. There it is a fool who ties the blindfold, and the point was satirical: justice that sees nothing. Only later was the blindfold reinterpreted as impartiality. Tarot kept the older image — justice that sees everything and still takes nobody’s side.

Waite left the other details without comment; his followers interpret them. The double-edged sword is read as a decision that cuts both ways and catches the one who hands it down. The white shoe, as a readiness to rise and act: the judge here not only weighs things up but also carries out the verdict.

Waite mentions mythology too: the female figure of this card “is said to be Astræa”, the goddess of justice. In Ovid, Astraea was the last of the immortals to leave the earth when people sank into violence, and legend made her the constellation Virgo. Waite immediately adds that the Tarot “is not of Roman mythology, or of Greek either”. Yet the image of the one who leaves last fits the eight remarkably well: it believes longer than anyone that things can still be settled fairly.

And one more detail from his book. Justice is one of the four cardinal virtues. The major arcana contain three of them: Justice, Strength and Temperance, numbered 8, 11 and 14 in the matrix. The fourth, Prudence, is missing from the deck; Waite suggests seeing an echo of it in the Hermit, “pursuing a solitary path by the light of his own lamp”. In the Marseille order the matrix counts by, [The Hermit](/encyclopedia/arcanum/9) comes straight after Justice.

sections.h2: What this reading is based on

ul: Arthur Edward Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910; reissued 1922): the symbolism of the card, the divinatory meanings upright and reversed, the remark on swapping VIII and XI, the passage on the virtues and Astraea.
Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015): justice as external, human-made balance, Newton’s third law, the comparison with Temperance, the Wheel of Fortune and The Lovers.
Yuliana Lisovskaya, Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost (The Destiny Matrix: Compatibility) (2024): the eighth energy in the compatibility matrix, retold in our own words.
The calculation follows Natalia Ladini’s classic destiny matrix scheme. The shares of people were counted by the site’s engine across all birth dates from 1 January 1900 to October 2026.
The legal principles are maxims of Roman law; the limitation period is Article 196 of the Civil Code of the Russian Federation.
The woodcut “A Fool Blindfolding Justice” is an illustration to Sebastian Brant’s Ship of Fools, Basel, 1494.
